messages.content: You write the short explanations that first-year programming students in India type when a C quiz asks them "Why did you choose that answer?". Reply with a JSON object only.

A student was shown this C code and question.

Code:
int i = 0;
while (i < 3) { fire(); }

Question: How many shots are fired?
The student answered: it never stops

The student understands this correctly: A loop variable only changes when the code changes it; with no update the condition stays true forever.

Write 5 different explanations this student might type for why they chose that answer.
Voice: long-winded, walks through the steps one by one, 20 to 35 words.

Rules:
- Each one must show the student's reasoning, not just repeat the answer.
- Write as the student, in the first person or with no subject. Do not judge the answer or say it is wrong.
- Do not name the idea as a rule and do not use textbook terms for the mistake.
- Make the 5 explanations differ in wording and in which part of the code they point at.

Return JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}

content: {"sentences": ["First I set i to 0, then the condition i less than 3 is true, so it enters the loop and calls fire, but nothing inside changes i back to 0 or anything.", "Look inside the curly braces: just fire() sits there, no i++ or i equals something, so after each shot we check i again and it is still 0.", "The while tests i < 3 at the top every single time. Since i started at 0 and no line inside touches i, that test keeps passing and fire keeps getting called.", "I traced it: i is 0, 0 is less than 3, fire runs, then loop again, i is still 0, fire runs, same thing, on and on with no way to reach 3.", "Nothing in the body moves i forward, so after each fire the condition reads the same 0, meaning the loop never finds a reason to exit and shots keep coming."]}

sentences: First I set i to 0, then the condition i less than 3 is true, so it enters the loop and calls fire, but nothing inside changes i back to 0 or anything.
Look inside the curly braces: just fire() sits there, no i++ or i equals something, so after each shot we check i again and it is still 0.
The while tests i < 3 at the top every single time. Since i started at 0 and no line inside touches i, that test keeps passing and fire keeps getting called.
I traced it: i is 0, 0 is less than 3, fire runs, then loop again, i is still 0, fire runs, same thing, on and on with no way to reach 3.
Nothing in the body moves i forward, so after each fire the condition reads the same 0, meaning the loop never finds a reason to exit and shots keep coming.
